etymology.text: Root ג־ד־ל, pattern קָטוֹל; related to Arabic جَدِل (jadil, “hard, strong, firm”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same root gives לְגַדֵּל “to raise (children), to grow (plants)”, גֹּדֶל “size” and מִגְדָּל “tower” — the name of Magdala, the town of Mary Magdalene, means “tower”.
pitfalls: The first vowel shortens in the other forms: גָּדוֹל → גְּדוֹלָה, גְּדוֹלִים, גְּדוֹלוֹת (ga- → g’-).
After a definite noun it takes the article too: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל “the big house”. Without it, הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל is a sentence: “the house is big”.
subtleties: Of people גָּדוֹל means “older, grown-up” (הָאָח הַגָּדוֹל “the older brother”), not “tall” — that is גָּבֹהַּ.
It also means “great, important” (סוֹפֵר גָּדוֹל), like German groß and Greek μεγάλος.

funFacts: קְטַנְטַנִּים “the little ones” is the everyday word for toddlers and their activities (a toddlers’ club, toddlers’ songs).

subtleties: Of family members קָטָן means “younger”: הָאָחוֹת הַקְּטַנָּה “the younger sister”.
קְטַנְטַן “teeny” repeats the last syllable — a common Hebrew way to make a diminutive.

etymology.text: Pattern קָטֹל; from the same root as Aramaic אריכא (’ariḵa, “long”) (Wiktionary). The root א־ר־ךְ also gives אֹרֶךְ “length”.

funFacts: The Biblical אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם “slow to anger” is literally “long of nostrils” — a nose that takes long to grow hot; German says langmütig.
pitfalls: The other forms take u and a doubled כּ: אֲרֻכָּה, אֲרֻכִּים, אֲרֻכּוֹת (arukà) — unpointed ארוכה, ארוכים.
Pointed with a short o (אָרֹךְ), written with ו: ארוך; the final letter is ךְ.
subtleties: It measures time too: שָׁבוּעַ אָרֹךְ “a long week”, שִׂיחָה אֲרֻכָּה “a long conversation”.

etymology.text: From the root ג־ב־הּ, which forms words about height; pattern קָטֹל (Wiktionary). The same root gives גֹּבַהּ “height”.

funFacts: The opposite is נָמוּךְ “low, short” — Hebrew measures people the way it measures walls: high or low.
pitfalls: The last letter is a sounded h: ה with a dot (mappiq) and a “stolen” a before it — gavóha. Unpointed: גבוה.
Of people גָּבֹהַּ is “tall”; גָּדוֹל of a person means “older, grown-up”.
subtleties: One word for “tall” and “high”: a tall man and a high price are both גָּבֹהַּ — where German says groß and hoch.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ṭāb- (“good”); cognate with Akkadian ṭābum and Arabic طَيِّب (ṭayyib) (Wiktionary). Root ט־ו־ב.

funFacts: Arabic طَيِّب is the same word (Turkish has it as the name Tayyip); German Masel and English mazel tov come from מַזָּל טוֹב.
pitfalls: As a reply טוֹב means “OK, fine” (טוֹב, אֲנִי בָּא); as an adverb it is “well”: הוּא מְבַשֵּׁל טוֹב “he cooks well”.
“Better” has no special form: טוֹב יוֹתֵר or יוֹתֵר טוֹב (lesson 17).
subtleties: טוֹב לִי means “I feel good / I’m fine (here)”; טוֹב שֶׁ… “it is good that …” (lesson 18).

funFacts: “Good and evil” in Hebrew is טוֹב וָרָע — the first two adjectives of this lesson, side by side in Genesis 2:9.
pitfalls: The feminine has a long a: רָעָה (raá) — and רָעָה is also a noun, “evil, misfortune”.
Do not confuse it with רֵעַ “friend, fellow” (Wiktionary): the same letters רע.
subtleties: Everyday Hebrew often says לֹא טוֹב “not good”: רַע sounds stronger, close to “evil”.

funFacts: The same root gives חֹדֶשׁ “month” (the “new” moon, lesson 15); Amharic አዲስ “new” is in Addis Ababa, “new flower”.
pitfalls: With the article it is הֶחָדָשׁ (הֶ, because ח cannot be doubled and its a is unstressed) — but הַחֲדָשָׁה, הַחֲדָשִׁים.
subtleties: חֲדָשׁוֹת, the feminine plural, also means “the news”.

examples.text: בַּבַּיִת הַיָּשָׁן שֶׁלָּנוּ הָיָה חֶדֶר גָּדוֹל.

etymology.text: Pattern קָטָל (Wiktionary, which gives no further etymology). Its letters are those of the verb יָשֵׁן “is asleep”.

funFacts: The Old City of Jerusalem is not “הָעִיר הַיְּשָׁנָה” but הָעִיר הָעַתִּיקָה, “the ancient city”.
pitfalls: Use יָשָׁן for things, זָקֵן (or politely מְבֻגָּר) for people: סֵפֶר יָשָׁן, but אִישׁ זָקֵן.
יָשָׁן “old” and יָשֵׁן “asleep, sleeps” are both written ישן: הַבַּיִת יָשָׁן “the house is old”, הַיֶּלֶד יָשֵׁן “the child is sleeping”.
subtleties: חָבֵר יָשָׁן is “an old (long-standing) friend”, not an elderly one.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ḏaḳan- (“beard”); cognate with Akkadian ziqnum and Arabic ذَقَن (ḏaqan) (Wiktionary) — the old man is “the bearded one”.

funFacts: זָקֵן comes from זָקָן “beard” — and Arabic ذَقَن means “chin”.
pitfalls: זָקֵן “old” and זָקָן “beard” differ only in the last vowel — both are written זקן.
To someone’s face זָקֵן can sound blunt; say מְבֻגָּר.
subtleties: In the Bible זְקֵנִים are the elders, a title of honour: זִקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Exodus 3:16).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses מְבֻגָּר as “adult, grown up, mature”; in Modern Hebrew it is also the polite everyday word for an old person (אָדָם מְבֻגָּר “an elderly person”), the reason it is taught here next to זָקֵן.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology; it files the word under the root ב־ג־ר (“to mature”). The form is a pu‘al participle: “matured”.

funFacts: The same root gives בַּגְרוּת “maturity” — and the Israeli school-leaving exams, the בַּגְרוּת (bagrut).
pitfalls: The feminine ends in -et: מְבֻגֶּרֶת, not *מְבֻגָּרָה.
Pointed with u (ֻ), written with ו: מבוגר, מבוגרת.
subtleties: It is the tactful word: לְאָדָם מְבֻגָּר “for an elderly person”, where זָקֵן could sound rude.
As “older than” it fits anyone: הִיא מְבֻגֶּרֶת מִמֶּנִּי בְּשָׁנָתַיִם “she is two years older than me”.

etymology.text: Compare Arabic حَمِيم (ḥamīm, “hot”) and Eblaite ḥammūtum (“hot”) (Wiktionary). Pattern קֶטֶל.

funFacts: Arabic حَمَّام “bath” (Turkish hamam) is built on the same Semitic root of heat, ח־מ־ם / ح-م-م.
pitfalls: “I am hot” is חַם לִי (“it is hot to me”), not *אֲנִי חַם.
The other forms double the מ: חַמָּה, חַמִּים, חַמּוֹת.
subtleties: With לְ the adjective stays masculine singular and tells how someone feels: חַם לָנוּ, חַם לָהּ.

etymology.text: Root ח־מ־ם, pattern קָטִיל (Wiktionary) — the same root as חַם “hot”.

funFacts: German warm / heiß = Hebrew חָמִים / חַם: one root, a gentler pattern. The Sabbath stew חַמִּין (hamin) is named for being kept hot.
pitfalls: חָמִים “warm” and חַמִּים “hot” (plural of חַם) are both written חמים: מַיִם חַמִּים “hot water”, but בַּיִת חָמִים “a warm home”.
With the article: הֶחָמִים, but הַחֲמִימָה.
subtleties: It is a positive word — the warmth you like; for the weather Israelis mostly just say חַם.

subtleties: יָפֶה also praises an action (“nice!, well done!”) and works as an adverb: הִיא שָׁרָה יָפֶה “she sings beautifully”.

funFacts: German hässlich comes from Hass “hate”; Hebrew has a root of its own for “ugly”, כ־ע־ר.

The feminine ends in -et: מְכֹעֶרֶת.
subtleties: About people it is harsh; Israelis soften it to לֹא כָּל כָּךְ יָפֶה “not so pretty”.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology. The verb הוֹזִיל “to make cheaper” and the noun הוֹזָלָה “price cut” are built on it.

funFacts: A common sign in Israeli shops: הַמְּחִירִים הוּזְלוּ “prices have been reduced” — the verb of זוֹל.
pitfalls: Of a price itself Hebrew prefers “low”: מְחִיר נָמוּךְ (as German niedriger Preis); זוֹל describes the thing: הַכַּרְטִיס זוֹל.
subtleties: זוֹל can sound pejorative (“cheap, tacky”); a positive “good value” is מִשְׁתַּלֵּם.

governs.none: takes no complement of its own (“than” in comparisons is מִ)

profile.feeling: Expensive taxis and dear friends.

examples.tr: Life in Tel Aviv is expensive.

Mum is very dear to me.
Dear friends, thank you for coming.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *waqar- (“to be heavy or weighty; to hold weight in value”), from Proto-Afroasiatic; compare Egyptian jqr (“excellent, worthy”) and Arabic وَقَار (waqār, “dignity”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Like German teuer, Greek ακριβός and Russian дорогой, יָקָר means both “expensive” and “dear”.
pitfalls: The first vowel shortens: יְקָרָה (yekará), יְקָרִים.
Not to be confused with קַר “cold”: יָקָר has a י at the start.
subtleties: In letters: יְקָרִי / יְקָרָתִי “my dear (m. / f.)”.

etymology.text: Root שׂ־מ־ח; inherited from Proto-Semitic; cognate with Ugaritic šmḫ (“to be glad, rejoice”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: שִׂמְחָה “joy” is also a name (Simcha), and שִׂמְחַת תּוֹרָה is the festival of “Rejoicing in the Torah”.
pitfalls: The final ח takes a “stolen” a: sa-mé-ach, pointed שָׂמֵחַ; in the other forms it is gone: שְׂמֵחָה.
“Glad to …” = שָׂמֵחַ לְ + infinitive; “glad that …” = שָׂמֵחַ שֶׁ… (lesson 18).
subtleties: שָׂמֵחַ is glad in the moment; מְאֻשָּׁר is happy with life.

profile.feeling: A sad face, a sad film, a sad song.

examples.text: הִיא עֲצוּבָה כִּי הַחֲבֵרָה שֶׁלָּהּ נָסְעָה.
examples.tr: She is sad because her friend has left.

etymology.text: Root ע־צ־ב (Wiktionary); the noun is עֶצֶב “sadness” (Wiktionary compares Arabic غَضَب, “anger”).

funFacts: עַצְבָּנִי “irritable, nervous” comes from עֲצַבִּים “nerves” — the same letters ע־צ־ב, but a different word from עֶצֶב “sadness”.
pitfalls: With the article: הֶעָצוּב, but הָעֲצוּבָה, הָעֲצוּבִים.
Feminine עֲצוּבָה (atsuvá) — the first a shortens.
subtleties: It describes what causes sadness as well: סִפּוּר עָצוּב “a sad story”.

profile.feeling: Tired after work, after a trip, after a long day.

senses.def: tired of, fed up with (עָיֵף מִ…)

examples.tr: I’m tired, I’m going to sleep.
She comes home tired from work.
The children are tired after the trip.
I’m tired of all the arguments.

etymology.text: Participle of the verb עִיֵּף; pattern קָטֵל (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Biblical word is the same: Esau comes in from the field “וְהוּא עָיֵף” — “and he was tired” (Genesis 25:29).
pitfalls: Pointed עָיֵף, but in full spelling it has two yods: עייף, עייפה.
With the article: הֶעָיֵף, but הָעֲיֵפָה.
subtleties: The noun is עֲיֵפוּת “tiredness”.

etymology.text: Root ר־ע־ב, pattern קָטֵל; related to Arabic رَغِبَ (raḡiba, “to desire”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The noun רָעָב “famine” is the famine that brought Jacob’s sons to Egypt (Genesis 41–42).
pitfalls: רָעֵב “hungry” and רָעָב “hunger, famine” differ only in the last vowel.
With the article: הָרָעֵב (ר takes הָ).
subtleties: The opposite is שָׂבֵעַ “full”: אֲנִי שָׂבֵעַ, תּוֹדָה “I’m full, thanks” is the polite way to refuse more food.

profile.feeling: Thirsty in an Israeli summer — always carry water.

examples.tr: I’m thirsty, is there any water?

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ṯ̣amiʔ- (“to thirst”); compare Arabic ظَمِئَ (ẓamiʔa, “to thirst; to long”) (Wiktionary). Pattern קָטֵל.

funFacts: Arabic ظَمْآن “thirsty” comes from the same Semitic root.
pitfalls: The final א is silent: tsamé; the feminine is tsme’á, צְמֵאָה.
subtleties: The noun is צָמָא “thirst” (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: An adjective in the קָטִיל pattern from the root מ־ה־ר, as the verb מִהֵר (“to hurry”); cognate with Arabic مَاهِر (māhir, “skilled, expert”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic مَاهِر “skilled” — and Turkish mahir “skilful”, from it — share this root; Hebrew kept both senses.
pitfalls: “Quickly” is the adverb מַהֵר, not מָהִיר: הוּא רָץ מַהֵר “he runs fast”.
subtleties: מָהִיר is about speed; “early” is a different word, מֻקְדָּם (lesson 14).

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym: Hebrew says אִטִּי for slow and the adverb לְאַט for slowly.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology. It is built on the adverb אַט “slowly, gently” (Wiktionary: אַט, לְאַט) with the adjective ending ־ִי.

funFacts: Biblical אַט means “gently”: David asks his men “לְאַט לִי לַנַּעַר לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם” — “deal gently, for my sake, with the young man Absalom” (2 Samuel 18:5).
pitfalls: The masculine plural has two yods: אִטִּיִּים (also written and said אִטִּים); the feminine ends in ־ִית: אִטִּית.
“Slowly” is the adverb לְאַט, not *אִטִּי.
subtleties: Adjectives in ־ִי take ־ִית in the feminine, like יִשְׂרְאֵלִי / יִשְׂרְאֵלִית.
